content:
Touma woke to find Mio standing in the corner.

Not her voice. Not the pressure of her attention somewhere behind his thoughts. Not a private comment waiting for him to become conscious enough to resent it.

Mio, in the corner, looking around the room as though she suspected it of having teeth.

He stared.

“You’re here,” he said.

“Yes.”

“No. You’re *there.*”

She looked down at herself, then back at him. “Apparently.”

The ceiling was still a suspicious beige. The broken lamp still leaned beside the futon. Dust, instant coffee, and cheap disinfectant still accounted for most of the room’s smell. Nothing had changed except that his private wrongness was now standing on the cheap rental carpet, like a clerical error large enough to become visible.

His face grew hot.

“Stop staring,” Mio said.

“I’m checking something.”

“What?”

“Whether you disappear when I blink.”

“Have you reached a conclusion?”

He blinked.

She remained.

“Unfortunately.”

Her expression sharpened.

“Not unfortunately that you’re—” He stopped. There had to be a way to finish that sentence without making it worse. He couldn’t find it.

Until now, there had been a layer between the strange things happening to him and the rest of the world. Thin, unreliable, humiliating in its own ways, but there. He could hear something no one else heard. He could answer under his breath and hope a clerk thought he was on a call. He could at least pretend the problem stopped at his skin.

Now it had a face, and the face was offended.

This was a rude way to wake up.

He pushed himself upright. Mio moved closer, then stopped beside the futon. There was something slightly wrong with the movement—a delay too small to call a stumble, as though the thought of moving had asked the room for permission before becoming motion.

Touma reached for the blanket bunched near her.

His hand passed through her knee.

He jerked it back.

For a moment, neither of them spoke. He had felt no resistance. That did not make it better. His eyes insisted he had done something his hand refused to remember.

Mio looked at her knee.

“Warn me before you do that.”

“I didn’t mean to.”

“That’s what makes it worse.”

He pulled his hand against his chest. “I was reaching for the blanket.”

“I understand where the blanket is.”

“Right.”

He waited until she had stepped away before touching it again.

New rules. There were going to be new rules for everything, apparently, including getting out of bed.

“Can you feel anything?” he asked.

Mio’s shoulders tightened.

“Physically or emotionally?”

“I meant—”

“Yes. That was the problem with the question.”

He dragged the blanket off his legs, carefully keeping it on his side of the available space.

“You could try not acting like a person who understands me too well.”

“That was always the case.”

It was. That was worse, too.

Memory returned in pieces: the procedure, instructions he had understood badly at the time, Nico’s face. A limiter. Something that was supposed to remain stable. He remembered enough to know this had a context, but not enough to make a girl standing beside his futon feel like a reasonable consequence.

She was more alive like this.

He didn’t like the comparison. Mio had been alive when she was only a voice. He hadn’t needed proof of that. But now he could see the small pause before she answered, the breath she seemed to take, the way she considered where to put her hands and then apparently rejected every option.

He could see her fear.

Not a confession of fear. Not something he had to infer from an unusually sharp remark.

It was there in her shoulders, in the attention she kept giving the door, in how carefully she stood still.

Touma looked away.

That felt wrong as well.

He got to his feet and began pacing the narrow strip between the futon and the kitchenette counter. There wasn’t enough room to do it properly. Three steps, turn, three steps back. The carpet scratched under his bare feet.

He kept looking at her.

He knew he was doing it. Knowing did not help. Each time he turned, his body checked where she was before deciding where he could go.

She had become the center of the room.

Not because she took up much space. He wasn’t even sure she took up space at all. But every movement now had to account for her. Where he stood. Where he looked. Whether he was too close. Whether turning his back would seem pointed.

Being watched by her had become physical.

“You’re doing it again,” Mio said.

“I know.”

“Does knowing usually help?”

“Not recently.”

He stopped at the counter, then immediately felt as though he had chosen the counter in order to stand farther away from her.

This wasn’t a tactical problem. He could have handled a tactical problem badly and at least understood what kind of failure he was having.

This was a social problem involving someone whose knee he had just put his hand through.

The door opened.

Touma turned too quickly.

Nico stopped in the doorway, one hand still on the handle. His eyes went to Touma, then Mio, then back to Touma with an effort that was almost more noticeable than staring would have been.

“You’re both awake.”

Touma looked at Mio.

“You knew she could do that?”

“No,” Nico said, too fast.

Mio folded her arms.

Nico took a breath. “Not like this.”

“That sounds like a different answer.”

“It’s a more precise answer.”

“You started with no.”

“Yes. I noticed.”

He still hadn’t come fully into the room.

Something from the procedure clicked into place in Touma’s memory. The visibility rule. A witness in range. Nico in the doorway wasn’t just Nico in the doorway.

Touma glanced at Mio again.

She was watching Nico with the same careful attention she had given the room.

“So that rule still applies,” Touma said.

“Yes,” Nico replied. “As far as we can tell.”

“As far as—”

“We have a limited amount of information.”

Mio’s mouth tightened. Nico saw it. Touma could tell because his grip shifted on the door handle.

It occurred to Touma that this was the first time Nico had been required to explain the problem outside a closed system while the problem stood there listening.

And could talk back.

“The limiter is stable for the moment,” Nico said. “The projection isn’t.”

“Projection,” Touma repeated.

“It’s the term we have.”

“You make it sound like a school presentation.”

“I’m trying to distinguish between the mechanism and the—”

“The person?” Mio asked.

Nico stopped.

Touma almost felt sorry for him.

Almost.

“The visible manifestation,” Nico said carefully, “appears to be a side effect.”

“The side effect is looking at you,” Touma said.

“I know.”

“And understands you.”

“I’m aware of that.”

“Then maybe be more precise.”

Nico looked at him. “That is what I’m attempting to do.”

“He is,” Mio said.

Touma turned toward her. “You’re taking his side?”

“I’m taking the side where we continue existing.”

That shut him up.

Nico finally released the handle. He didn’t move farther into the room.

“There’s another issue.”

“Of course there is,” Touma said.

“If she can manifest outside the system, other systems may be able to register her now.”

Touma’s glance went automatically to the ceiling.

Nothing there but beige paint and an old stain. He looked anyway.

“What systems?”

“Cameras. Biometrics. Active recognition filters.”

The room seemed to lose another layer of privacy.

Touma thought of walking back past the clerk. Of a camera over a counter recording him with someone who shouldn’t have been there. Something noticing a face, comparing it, keeping the result. His embarrassment no longer needed another person in the room to become a problem.

“People?” he asked.

“Possibly,” Nico said. “We don’t know how broadly this carries.”

Touma looked at Mio. Her hands were still tucked beneath her arms. Now he could see how tightly she held them there.

“How bad is that?”

Nico’s eyes moved toward her once more before settling on him.

“Bad enough for you.”
